故人的怀表
The name of this Relic has bothered me for far too long. Help?
GTL outputs "An Old Friend's Pocket Watch." Keeping the setting on "Chinese (Simplified)" does keep the meaning of these words when separated (故人 "an old friend" & 的怀表 "pocket watch") but when it's set to "Detect language," it sees this word 故人 as Japanese and outputs "deceased," with "old friend" as an alternative translation.

The game has this translated as "Deceased's Chrono," which... bleh.
I think the flavor text shines some more light on the meaning. There's 3 fairly similar translations I'm getting, so I'll give all 3.
肩负着怀念与感伤，向未知前进。
"Bearing memories and sorrow, we move forward into the unknown."
"Bearing the weight of nostalgia and sorrow, moving forward into the unknown."
"Carrying memories and sorrow, moving toward the unknown." (this is from in-game)

My initial re-phrasing of the name was going to be "Dead-Man's Timepiece," but having looked into it, it's very clear to me the fact that said person was *a friend* got lost in translation. In its depiction it's closed, and the initials (does "FJ" have any meaning I'm missing?) insinuate it's simply a watch that belonged to said FJ, and not the kind you would put an image of said friend inside of.

So my question is, how important is the insinuation that said friend is dead? Can the flavor text carry that information if tweaked a bit? What would be a good translation of this? 
The only term I'm aware we have in English that would apply is "Late Friend" as "Late" insinuates that the friend has passed. Initially I thought "Late Friend's Timepiece" sounded a little awkward, but honestly I like the double-entendre of "Late" also meaning that said friend is just tardy to an event, and I think would make good flavor text hit harder once it clarifies the definition.

Although the term 故人 is written with the same Chinese characters throughout East Asia, its meaning differs by country. In Korea and Japan, it is most commonly understood to mean "a deceased person", whereas in China it is more commonly understood to mean "an old friend" or "a longtime acquaintance".
So... I think it would be more appropriate to preserve the nuance of "an old friend."
So would "Late Friend" be too close to that other meaning? Should we use "Old Friend" instead?
I think so, but i'm sure since i'm not a native Chinese either
understandable lol

Okay, for now I'll go with:

**Old Friend's Timepiece**
> Bearing the bittersweet nostalgia of good times past, moving unceasingly into an unknown future.

Definitely chime in with any other opinions!
故人 in Chinese is also "a deceased person". And "former wife/husband".
So keeping only "deceased" would be more correct.

Okay! But using "deceased" as this kind of noun is incredibly odd, so while my question about the meaning of 故人 is answered, I'm still back to square 1 in terms of what this should be in English.

I think my take on the flavor text is good regardless of what we pick. Would "Late Friend" work?

-# also I realize going with "Timepiece" is kind of an arbitrary decision on my part, considering it is literally a pocket watch. I just figured there were multiple relics already called "pocketwatch" so I could diversify it since this one didn't end up "pocketwatch" but they do all use this word 怀表 so idk
What about "departed"?

Still feels like too much of an adjective, and I don't want to make the Relic's name *too* long. If we wanted to use Deceased or Departed alone as the identifying descriptor for the owner of this item, writing it properly would be "Pocketwatch *of the* Deceased/Departed" which also feels wrong because it's easier to read that as a collective noun

But if we were fine with using Friend in conjunction here, "Deceased/Departed Friend's" would and should be cut to just "Dead Friend's" which at that point I still think "Late Friend's Pocketwatch" would work better

Old Friend or Dear Friend would also work, but wouldn't carry the explicit meaning of the item's owner being dead
